'''Blackrock National Hurling Club''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club located in [[Blackrock, Cork|Blackrock]], [[Cork (city)|Cork]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club is affiliated to the [[Seandún GAA|Seandún Board]] and the [[Cork GAA|Cork County Board]]. As a sister club of [[St Michael's GAA (Cork)|St Michael's Gaelic Football Club]], Blackrock is solely concerned with [[hurling]].

==Foundation==

Located in the fishing village of [[Blackrock, Cork|Blackrock]], to the southeast of [[Cork (city)|Cork]], a hurling club known as Cork Nationals was established in 1883, some 18 months before the foundation of the [[Gaelic Athletic Association]]. Hurling had been played in the area long before this, with reports of a match being played against [[St Finbarr's National Hurling & Football Club]] in October 1876. The club changed its name in 1888 to National Hurling Club, Blackrock, before later adopting the name Blackrock National Hurling Club.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.blackrockhurlingclub.com/history|title=History|publisher=Blackrock GAA website|date=|access-date=30 December 2025}}</ref>

==History==

Cork Nationals were the inaugural [[Cork Senior Hurling Championship|Cork SHC]] winners in 1887, however, they were declared the champions without having to play [[Passage West GAA|Passage]] in the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/sport/histrionics-a-founding-aspect-to-a-rivalry-that-has-real-history-but-least-we-can-expect-a-game-now-1.634844|title=Histrionics a founding aspect to a rivalry that has real history, but least we can expect a game now|publisher=Irish Times|date=7 August 2010|access-date=10 November 2017}}</ref> In spite of this inauspicious start, the club quckly became the preeminent team in the championship and claimed eight Cork SHC titles from nine final appearances between 1887 and 1898.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hoganstand.com/Cork/ClubTitles|title=Club Titles - Cork|publisher=Hogan Stand|date=|access-date=30 December 2025}}</ref> Such was Blackrock's dominance of the local hurling scene that their second team also claimed the [[Cork Junior Hurling Championship|Division 2]] title in [[1895 Cork Junior Hurling Championship|1895]]. Blackrock, as the [[Cork GAA|Cork]] inter-county representatives, also won consecutive [[All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship|All-Ireland SHC]] titles in [[1893 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship|1893]] and [[1894 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship|1894]], following respective and comprehensive defeats of [[Kilkenny GAA|Kilkenny]] and [[Dublin GAA|Dublin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport-columnists/arid-41429941.html|title=Paul Rouse: In 1893 All-Ireland final, Cork robbed by Dublin ref: same as it ever was...|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=5 July 2024|access-date=4 October 2025|first=|last=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dublingaa.ie/news/recent-meetings-dublin-v-cork-hurling|title=Recent meetings: Dublin v Cork (hurling)|publisher=Dublin GAA website|date=29 July 2021|access-date=30 December 2025}}</ref>

The early years of the 20th century brought a third All-Ireland SHC for Blackrock, after beating [[London GAA|London]] by 3–16 to 1–01 in the [[1903 All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship final|1903 All-Ireland SHC final]]. The club also continued its dominance of the local championship and had amassed 15 Cork SHC titles by 1920. This represented just under half of all the available titles since 1887 and three times as many as [[St. Finbarr's GAA|St Finbarr's]] and [[Redmonds GAA|Redmonds]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-40058756.html|title=Glen Rovers v Blackrock: A reminder of the halcyon days of Cork hurling|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=2 October 2020|access-date=30 December 2025}}</ref> Blackrock set a new record in 1931, with [[Eudie Coughlan]] captaining the team to a fourth consecutive Cork SHC title - their 21st title overall - after a 2–04 to 0–03 win over [[Éire Óg GAA (Cork)|Éire Óg]]. After dominating the Cork SHC since its inception, it would be 25 years before a [[Mick Cashman]]-captained Blackrock team won their 22nd title, after beating [[Glen Rovers GAA|Glen Rovers]] by 2–10 to 2–02 in the [[1956 Cork Senior Hurling Championship|1956 final]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-41351407.html|title=Blackrock National Hurling Club celebrate a glorious history with anniversary event|publisher=Echo Live|date=14 March 2024|access-date=30 December 2025}}</ref>

The 1970s saw Blackrock emerge with a new team featuring [[John Horgan (hurler)|John Horgan]], [[Tom Cashman]], [[Pat Moylan (Cork hurler)|Pat Moylan]] and the Cummins brothers - [[Brendan Cummins (Cork hurler)|Brendan]] and [[Ray Cummins|Ray]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-41127217.html|title=Throwback Thursday: Blackrock golden age began with All-Ireland success in 1972 |date=4 May 2023|publisher=Echo Live|access-date=24 December 2025|first=Dylan|last=O'Connell}}</ref> Five Cork SHC

'''Newport GAA''' is a [[Tipperary GAA]] club which is located in [[County Tipperary]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. Both [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]] are played in the [[North Tipperary GAA|North Tipperary]] divisional competitions. The club is centred on the town of [[Newport, County Tipperary|Newport]].

==Lacken Park==
Named after [[Patrick Ryan (Irish politician)|Paddy Ryan Lacken]], and known locally as "The Park". It has four changing rooms (Home on right). With a club house at the end with many Newport GAA memorabilia as well as a kitchen a Referee's room while a meeting room also in the building. There are three pitches, a main pitch with a stand and great floodlight facilities. Separating the two Juvenile pitches and the main pitch is a hurling wall. The Juvenile pitch is very well designed with "The Hill" behind the far goal where the younger supporters watch on from. The Juvenile pitch is also floodlit, while the even younger teams (U8-10) play in a junior pitch with smaller goals and a shorter pitch. The U8-10s train in the GYM in the winter beside St. Mary's Secondary School. While the rest train in the Ball Alleys beside Newport College (Vocational School) in Newport, while the pitch is unplayable.

'''UCD GAA''' or '''University College Dublin Gaelic Athletic Association club''' is a [[Dublin]] based [[Gaelic games]] club in [[University College Dublin]]. The UCD [[hurling]] club was founded in 1900 and boasted the mottos "Ad Astra" and "Cothrom Féinne". The first team was an amalgamation of students from UCD and Cecilia St. Although UCD had been playing [[Gaelic football]] unofficially since 1900, the official club history began in the season of 1911/1912.

The football club competes in the [[Sigerson Cup]] and Higher Education Leagues as well as in the [[Dublin Senior Football Championship]] and the [[O'Byrne Cup]]. The hurling club competes in the [[Fitzgibbon Cup]] and Higher Education Leagues and occasionally in the [[Dublin Senior Hurling Championship]] and the [[Walsh Cup (hurling)|Walsh Cup]]. The Camogie Club competes in the [[Ashbourne Cup]]. The [[ladies Gaelic football]] team competes in the [[HEC O'Connor Cup|O'Connor Cup]].

Former [[Dublin county football team|Dublin]] footballer [[Brian Mullins]] was the director of Sports at UCD.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20030308164152/http://www.cusai.ie/members/brianmullins.html ]</ref> * [[Ger Brennan]] & Josh Warde are currently in charge of all Gaelic games on the UCD campus.<ref>[http://www.ucd.ie/sport/theteam.htm UCD – Sport<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

==Hurling==
UCD won the [[Leinster Senior Hurling Championship]] and the [[All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship|All-Ireland]] representing [[Dublin GAA|Dublin]] as the Collegians in 1917. In the all-Ireland final, the Collegians beat [[Boherlahan-Dualla GAA|Boherlahan]] of [[Tipperary GAA|Tipperary]] by a score-line of 5–4 to 4–2 at [[Croke Park]]. The attendance was 11,000. The Collegians all-Ireland winning team were: [[Tommy Daly|T. Daly]], [[John Ryan (Dublin hurler)|J. Ryan]], S. Hyde, S. O’Donavon, H. Burke, C. Stuart, J. Phelan, [[Bob Mockler|B. Mockler]], [[Tommy Moore (hurler)|T. Moore]], J. Cleary, F. Burke, M. Neville, M. Hackett, M. Hayes, P. Kenefick. Sub: [[Brendan Considine|B. Considine]].

More recently, UCD won the 2000, 2004 and 2005 [[Dublin Senior Hurling Championship]]s and reached the [[Leinster Senior Club Hurling Championship]] final on each occasion but were defeated by narrow margins.

In 2004, UCD won the [[Walsh Cup (hurling)|Walsh Cup]] for the first time when they convincingly beat reigning [[All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship|All-Ireland]] champions, [[Kilkenny GAA|Kilkenny]], by 2–16 to 0–5.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.breakingnews.ie/archives/2004/0207/sport/ucd-claim-walsh-cup-133138.html|title=UCD claim Walsh Cup|date=7 February 2004|access-date=6 March 2011}}</ref>

UCD last won the [[Fitzgibbon Cup]] in 2001 when they were captained by David Hegarty ([[Clare GAA|Clare]]). They defeated [[University College Cork|UCC]] in the final. Team: Matty White, Robbie Kirwan, DOC O'Connor, Brian Walton, Colm Everard, David Hegarty, Hugh Flannery, Gary Mernagh, Stephen Lucey, Pat Fitzgerald, Sean O'Neill, Redmond Barry, Brendan Murphy, Alan Barry, John Culkin.

'''Na Piarsaigh Hurling and Football Club''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in Fair Hill, [[Cork (city)|Cork]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club is affiliated to the [[Seandún GAA|Seandún Board]] and fields teams in both [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]].

==History==

Located in the Fair Hill area on the northside of [[Cork (city)|Cork]], Na Piarsaigh Hurling and Football Club was founded by a group of [[North Monastery]] students in 1943.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40353743.html|title=Cork GAA Jersey Wars: Na Piarsaigh v Charleville|publisher=Echo Live|date=31 August 2020|access-date=18 April 2022|first=|last=}}</ref> The club is named in honour of [[Pádraig Pearse]], to reflect the [[Irish nationalism|nationalist]] ideals of the club and its members. Early training sessions took place at [[Collins Barracks, Cork|Collins Barracks]], prior to the club acquiring their own playing field in 1951.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://napiarsaigh.com/about-us/|title=Our story|publisher=Na Piarsaigh GAA website|date=|access-date=13 June 2025|first=|last=}}</ref>

Na Piarsaigh had their first success when, in 1946, they claimed their [[Cork City Junior A Hurling Championship|City JHC]] title.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://seandungaa.ie/roll-of-honour-jahc-winners/|title=Roll Of Honour JAHC Winners|publisher=Seandún GAA website|date=|access-date=13 June 2025|first=|last=}}</ref> Their second title, won in 1953, was subsequently converted into a [[Cork Junior Hurling Championship|Cork JHC]], following a 6-00	to 2–10 win over [[Cloughduv GAA|Cloughduv]] in the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40103342.html|title=Na Piarsaigh versus Glen Rovers: The great northside hurling rivalry |publisher=Echo Live|date=29 August 2020|access-date=18 April 2022|first=|last=}}</ref> Na Piarsaigh made a Gaelic football breakthrough in 1964, with the first of back-to-back [[Cork City Junior A Football Championship|City JAFC]] titles.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://seandungaa.ie/roll-of-honour-jafc-winners/|title=Roll Of Honour JAFC Winners|publisher=Seandún GAA website|date=|access-date=13 June 2025|first=|last=}}</ref> The [[Cork Junior A Football Championship|Cork JFC]] was won in 1965, while the club secured a second successive promotion by claiming the [[Cork Intermediate Football Championship|Cork IFC]] in 1966, thus becoming a [[Dual player|dual]] senior club.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dohenygaa.com/page/1965-extra-time-28.aspx|title=1965 Extra Time|publisher=Dohenys GAA website|date=|access-date=28 November 2021|first=|last=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-20210141.html|title=Masterful McEnery keeps Nick’s in top flight|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=8 October 2012|access-date=19 July 2022|first=|last=}}</ref>

The club was also successful on the underage front, winning numerous Cork MHC and MFC titles, as well as several [[Cork Under-21 Hurling Championship|Cork U21HC]] titles between the 1960s and 1980s. These successes paved the way for the club's first ever [[Cork Senior Hurling Championship|Cork SHC]] title, won in 1990 after a 2–07 to 1–08 defeat of [[St. Finbarr's GAA|St Finbarr's]] in the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40122080.html|title=Classic Cork county hurling finals: The day Na Piarsaigh joined the top table|publisher=Echo Live|date=1 May 2020|access-date=18 April 2022|first=John|last=Horgan}}</ref> Na Piarsaigh won their second Cork SHC title after beating [[Ballyhea GAA|Ballyhea]] in the 1995 final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40098986.html|title=Na Piarsaigh recall great victory of 1995 while remembering fallen comrades|publisher=Echo Live|date=30 September 2020|access-date=9 August 2021}}</ref> The club maintained their perfect record in SHC finals in 2004, by beating [[Cloyne GAA|Cloyne]] by 0–17 to 0–10 to collect their third title.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irishexaminer.com/archives/2004/1101/world/piarsaigh-storm-to-cork-title-437896262.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808050303/http://www.irishexaminer.com/archives/2004/1101/world/piarsaigh-storm-to-cork-title-437896262.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=8 August 2014|title=Piarsaigh storm to Cork title|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=1 November 2004|access-date=16 December 2017|first=Diarmuid|last=O'Flynn}}</ref>

The club's crest features the [[Red Hand of Ulster|red hand of Ulster]], with the thumb omitted. According to the club, the omission of the thumb "symbolises the six northern counties 'under foreign rule'" and that, in the event of a [[United Ireland]], "the thumb will rejoin the fingers to create a strong, powerful, useful hand".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Moynihan |first=Adam |date=2024-12-25 |title=We looked at every GAA crest in the world — here’s what we found |url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-41521391.html |access-date=2026-10-27 |website=Irish Examiner |language=en}}</ref>

'''Sarsfields GAA''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Glanmire]], [[County Cork]], Ireland. The club, a sister club of [[Glanmire GFC|Glanmire]], is solely concerned with the game of [[hurling]].

==History==

Sarsfields GAA Club was established by a group of men, led by [[Willie O'Neill (Cork hurler)|Billy O'Neill]], in 1894. Named in honour of the Irish [[Jacobitism|Jacobite]] and soldier [[Patrick Sarsfield, 1st Earl of Lucan]], the club was first formally registered in 1896.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40112300.html|title=Sars mourn the loss of club legend Dave McCarthy|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Echo Live|date=28 June 2020}}</ref> Sarsfields claimed their first county honours in 1937, when the [[Cork Junior Hurling Championship|Cork JHC]] was secured, however, there were also [[Cork Premier Senior Hurling Championship#List of finals|Cork SHC final]] defeats in 1909, 1936, 1940, 1947 and 1989.<ref name="SHCrollofhonour"/>

Sarsfields made the SHC breakthrough in 1951 following a 5–08 to 3–07 defeat of [[Glen Rovers GAA|Glen Rovers]] in the [[1951 Cork Senior Hurling Championship#Final|final]]. The club added a second SHC title after a defeat of [[UCC GAA|University College Cork]] in 1957.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-20073342.html|title=Sars likely to have too much, but Rovers will prove tough test|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=27 September 2008}}</ref> A fallow period in terms of success followed for the next 50 years before the club's "golden era".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40123646.html|title=Classic Cork county hurling finals: 51 years of emotion poured out for Sars|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Echo Live|date=2 May 2020}}</ref> In the eight-year period between 2008 and 2015, Sarsfields contested seven SHC finals,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-41259475.html|title=Sars aiming to improve Cork's dreadful Munster Hurling championship record|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=1 November 2023}}</ref> with victories in 2008, 2010, 2012 and 2014.<ref name="SHCrollofhonour"/>

Sarsfields collected their seventh Cork SHC title after a 0–21 to 0–19 defeat of [[Midleton GAA|Midleton]] in 2023.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-41248528.html|title=Sars eventually find their feet to secure first Cork SHC title in nine years|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=15 October 2023|access-date=15 October 2023|first=Eoghan|last=Cormican}}</ref> Days after this victory the club suffered extensive damage to their club grounds and main pitch after [[Storm Babet]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/news/munster/arid-41250886.html|title='We are all just devastated': Historic Cork hurling club badly damaged by Storm Babet|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=19 October 2023}}</ref> Sarsfields won the [[Munster Senior Club Hurling Championship|Munster Club SHC]] title after a 3–20 to 2–19 win over [[Ballygunner GAA|Ballygunner]] in 2024.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-games/hurling/ballygunner-blitzed-by-shane-oregan-as-sarsfields-land-first-title/a1777087148.html|title=Ballygunner blitzed by Shane O'Regan as Sarsfields land first title|access-date=2 December 2024|publisher=Irish Independent|date=2 December 2024}}</ref>

==Grounds==

The club's home ground is Páirc Tadhg Mac Cárthaigh.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-41607910.html|title=First look at Sarsfields' 'really, really right' Teddy McCarthy statue|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=6 April 2025|access-date=22 September 2025|first=|last=}}</ref> It was renamed in honour of former player [[Teddy McCarthy]], who was a dual All-Ireland medal-winner in 1990. The official renaming ceremony took place on 5 April 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-41607808.html|title=A perfect day in Riverstown as hundreds attend unveiling of Teddy McCarthy statue|publisher=Echo Live|date=6 April 2025|access-date=22 September 2025|first=|last=}}</ref>

'''Patrickswell GAA''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Patrickswell]], [[County Limerick]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club is primarily concerned with the game of [[hurling]], but has also fielded teams in [[Gaelic football]].

==History==

Located in the village of [[Patrickswell]], about 10km outside [[Limerick (city)|Limerick]], Patrickswell GAA Club was founded in 1943.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.patrickswellgaa.com/history/|title=History|publisher=Patrickswell GAA website|date=|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref> The club spent its early existence operating in the junior grades, winning [[Limerick Junior Hurling Championship|Limerick JAHC]] titles in 1955 and 1957. This was followed by a Limerick JAFC title in 1964. After voting to remain in the senior grade, Patrickswell made the breakthrough by winning consecutive [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|Limerick SHC]] titles in 1965 and 1966.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-40728309.html|title='Some people might not like me saying this, but Patrickswell-Kilmallock is a real traditional final'|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=24 October 2021|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref>

After their initial title success, Patrickswell proceeded to dominate the local club hurling scene. 16 titles were claimed between 1965 and 1997 to put them equal with all-time record holders [[Ahane GAA|Ahane]]. The club also won two [[Munster Senior Club Hurling Championship|Munster Club SHC]] titles during that period, as well as losing to [[Glenmore GAA|Glenmore]] in the [[1991 All-Ireland Senior Club Hurling Championship final|1991 All-Ireland club final]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://munster.gaa.ie/history/shclub_teams/|title=Senior Hurling (Club)|publisher=Munster GAA website|date=|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=|last=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-games/hurling/dermot-crowe-fallen-giants-restoring-parish-pride-after-wilderness-years/34430005.html|title=Dermot Crowe: Fallen giants restoring parish pride after wilderness years|publisher=Irish Independent|date=7 February 2016|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=|last=}}</ref>

Patrickswell and Ahane continued their battle to be outright leaders on the all-time roll of honour at the turn of the century. After a 13-year lapse, Patrickswell drew level once again after claiming their 19th Limerick SHC title in 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/breakingnews/sport/patrickswell-dominate-ballybrown-to-capture-19th-limerick-shc-title-760623.html|title=Patrickswell dominate Ballybrown to capture 19th Limerick SHC title|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=23 October 2016|access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref> Patrickswell beat [[Na Piarsaigh GAA (Limerick)|Na Piarsaigh]] by 1-17 to 0-15 to claim a record 20th SHC title in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-games/hurling/cian-lynch-comes-to-the-fore-as-patrickswell-hold-off-na-piarsaigh-in-limerick-county-final-38567636.html|title=Cian Lynch comes to the fore as Patrickswell hold off Na Piarsaigh in Limerick county final|publisher=Irish Independent|date=6 October 2019|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=Colm|last=Keys}}</ref>

'''South Liberties ''' (Irish: ''Saor Theas'') is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club based in [[County Limerick]], Ireland. The club is based in the parish of Donoughmore-Knockea-Roxboro, on the southern outskirts of Limerick City and is affiliated to the East Board of [[Limerick GAA]]. It is one of the oldest clubs in the country, founded in 1884, the same year as the GAA. South Liberties' home ground in Ballysheedy is called Dooley Park, in memory of one of the club's greatest players. The club has won many county titles during its history, most notably seven [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship]]s; in 1888, 1889, 1890, 1972, 1976, 1978 and 1981. The club currently fields teams in the Senior [[hurling]] and Junior [[Gaelic football]] championships in Limerick.

==History==
The club was founded in May 1884 when a group of people in the Ballysheedy area of [[County Limerick]] got together to play hurling. The club name reflects its location in the former "south liberties of Limerick";<ref>Greensmyth, H. (Ed.), ''Up The Souths – History of South Liberties GAA Club'', Salesian Press Trust, Pallaskenry, 1984, p.27.</ref> this was the portion of the [[county of the city]] of [[Limerick]] outside the municipal boundary and south of the [[River Shannon]], which was transferred to County Limerick in 1842.<ref>
{{cite book |title=The Statutory Rules and Orders Revised, being the Statutory Rules and Orders (Other Than Those of a Local, Personal Or Temporary Character) in force on December 31, 1903 |volume=2 |edition=2nd |chapter=County (Ireland); (q) Limerick County and Limerick City |chapter-url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hl562h;view=1up;seq=783 |page=71 |access-date=11 July 2016 |year=1904 |publisher=H.M. Stationery Office }} 
</ref> The boundaries of the liberties were marked with 'Liberty Stones' and the club has incorporated an image of the sole surviving stone into its crest. South Liberties' home ground in Ballysheedy is called Dooley Park, in memory of one of the club's greatest players. Johnny Dooley played for Liberties from the mid-1940s to 1970, when he died suddenly after playing in a county championship match. He was on the Limerick teams that won the [[All-Ireland Junior Hurling Championship]]s of 1948, 1954 and 1957.

In the early days of the GAA, South Liberties were one of Limerick's greatest teams and contested the first five county finals, winning three of them in successive years, 1888–1890. A remarkable feature about these wins was that two of them were secured by the only score of an hour's hurling – one point in each case; made more remarkable by the fact that these games were played in the days when each side had 21 players and there were point posts at both sides of the goal, covering almost half of the end-line. On both occasions the point was scored by the same player, Con Sheehan, with Liberties defeating Murroe at [[Croom]] on 15 May 1888 and Kilfinane at [[Charleville, County Cork|Ráth Luirc]] on 13 July 1890. He also scored in the 1889 final when Liberties beat [[Caherline GAA|Caherline]] 1–2 to 0–3 at Croom on 13 July.<ref>[http://www.askaboutireland.ie/aai-files/assets/libraries/limerick-city-library/reading-room/sport/con-sheehan.pdf O' Ceallaigh, Seamus, ''Great Limerick Sportsmen. No. 65 John O'Connell of South Liberties''], Limerick Leader, 6 February 1954. Retrieved 15 December 2009.</ref> John (Jack) Malone captained the Liberties' teams in all five finals.<ref>[http://www.askaboutireland.ie/aai-files/assets/libraries/limerick-city-library/reading-room/sport/john-malone.pdf O' Ceallaigh, Seamus, ''Great Limerick Sportsmen. No. 150 John Malone of South Liberties''], Limerick Leader, 1 October 1955. Retrieved 15 December 2009.</ref> Many of the players that featured on those teams were forced to emigrate in the early 1890s and this coupled with the devastating effect that the Parnell Split had on GAA clubs meant that South Liberties ceased to be a force in Limerick hurling for another 75 years.<ref>[http://www.askaboutireland.ie/aai-files/assets/libraries/limerick-city-library/reading-room/sport/john-oconnell.pdf O' Ceallaigh, Seamus, ''Great Limerick Sportsmen. No. 214 Con Sheehan of South Liberties''], Limerick Leader, 1 March 1958. Retrieved 15 December 2009.</ref>

[[File:Dooley Park.jpg|left|thumb|Clubhouse at Dooley Park]]

'''Mallow GAA''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club based in the town of [[Mallow, County Cork|Mallow]], [[County Cork]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club fields teams in [[hurling]], [[Gaelic football]], [[Camogie]] and Ladies Gaelic Football ([[Ladies' Gaelic Football Association|LGFA]]).

The club's [[hurling]] team competes in the [[Cork Intermediate A Hurling Championship]] having been relegated from the Cork Premier Intermediate Hurling Championship in 2025. The club's [[Gaelic football]] team competes in the [[Cork Premier Senior Football Championship]] having won the [[Cork Senior A Football Championship]] in 2021.

==History==

Founded in 1887, the Mallow club enjoyed its first success at adult level when the [[Cork Junior Hurling Championship|Cork JHC]] title was won after a defeat of Rangers in 1914. Further success followed when the [[Cork Intermediate Hurling Championship|Cork IHC]] was claimed in 1923, giving the club [[Cork Senior Hurling Championship|senior status]] for the first time.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://homepage.eircom.net/~kod/intermediate_hurling_1.htm|title=Intermediate Hurling Finals 1909 - 1969|publisher=Cork GAA Finals website|access-date=15 December 2017}}</ref> Mallow's time in the top flight saw them record one of the biggest shocks in the first 50 years of the championship when they beat 18-time and reigning champions [[Blackrock GAA|Blackrock]] in the [[1928 Cork Senior Hurling Championship#Second round|1928 second round]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40353749.html|title=Cork GAA Jersey Wars: Cill na Martra v Mallow|publisher=Echo Live|date=14 August 2021|accessdate=12 November 2022|first=Denis|last=Hurley}}</ref> They were subsequently beaten by [[Éire Óg GAA (Cork)|Éire Óg]] in their only appearance in a senior final.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.eireogcork.ie/contentPage/344995/c_l_u_b_h_i_s_t_o_r_y|title=Éire Óg – Club History|publisher=Éire Óg GAA website|date=|accessdate=12 November 2017|first=|last=}}</ref> In spite of this, Mallow claimed further Cork IHC titles in 1959 and 1972.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/regionals/corkman/localnotes/golden-memories-promised-as-mallow-fetes-team-of-59-27073697.html|title=Golden memories promised as Mallow fetes team of '59|publisher=The Corkman|access-date=16 December 2017|date=26 November 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://homepage.eircom.net/~kod/intermediate_hurling_2.htm|title=Intermediate Hurling Finals 1970 - 2003|publisher=Cork GAA Finals website|access-date=17 October 2020}}</ref>

Mallow's second century saw the club enjoy many Gaelic football successes. A [[Cork Intermediate Football Championship|Cork IFC]] title in 1992 was followed by [[Cork Premier Intermediate Football Championship|Cork PIFC]] triumphs in 2007 and 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hoganstand.com/county/cork/article/index/90288|title=United Mallow stand|publisher=Hogan Stand|date=20 February 2008|access-date=19 July 2022|first=|last=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irishexaminer.com/ireland/mallow-dig-deep-45828.html|title=Mallow dig deep|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=22 October 2007|accessdate=16 October 2017|first=Bob|last=Lester|archive-date=17 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171017043918/http://www.irishexaminer.com/ireland/mallow-dig-deep-45828.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/football/heartbreak-for-st-michaels-as-mallow-win-cork-premier-intermediate-final-460952.html|title=Heartbreak for St Michael's as Mallow win Cork Premier Intermediate final|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=16 October 2017|accessdate=13 November 2019|first=Therese|last=O'Callaghan}}</ref> Mallow claimed their first ever senior title when they beat [[St Michael's GAA (Cork)|St. Michael's]] to take the [[Cork Senior A Football Championship|Cork SAFC]] title in 2021.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40754556.html|title=SAFC: Seán Hayes on target at death to give Mallow victory over St Michael's|publisher=Echo Live|date=28 November 2021|access-date=28 November 2021|first=Denis|last=Hurley}}</ref>

In 2022, a Seven-goal blitz saw Mallow win the Minor Hurling Challenge Cup at Páirc Uí Rinn beating their opponents Inniscarra on a scoreline of Mallow 7-14 Inniscarra 0-13. [https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-40975466.html]

'''UCC''' is a football and hurling club associated with [[University College Cork]]. UCC teams play in the [[Cork Senior Football Championship]] and [[Cork Senior Hurling Championship]] as well as the two main third-level competitions namely the [[Sigerson Cup]] in football, the [[Fitzgibbon Cup]] in hurling and the [[Ashbourne Cup]] in camogie.  They also competed against inter-county sides in the pre-season [[McGrath Cup]] (football) and [[Waterford Crystal Cup]] (hurling).<ref>{{cite news|author=Christmas tips |url=http://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-football/ucc-march-past-banner-to-semis-117765.html |title=UCC march past Banner to semis - Gaelic Football - Independent.ie |publisher=Independent.ie |date= 2006-01-16|access-date=2008-12-28}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Sonia down under |url=http://www.independent.ie/sport/hurling/callanan-shines-as-tipp-ease-past-ucc-1265510.html |title=Callanan shines as Tipp ease past UCC - Hurling - Independent.ie |publisher=Independent.ie |date= 2008-01-14|access-date=2008-12-28}}</ref> The piratical skull and crossbones logo on the team shirt, which first appeared on the rugby team of what was then known as Queen’s College Cork (composed mostly of medical students, hence the bones) was appropriated in the mid-1910s by the GAA clubs, and in 1929 by the UCC hockey club.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.balls.ie/gaa/the-brilliant-story-behind-the-ucc-skull-and-crossbones-aka-the-best-gaa-jersey-ever-324294|title= The Brilliant Story Behind The UCC Skull And Crossbones, AKA The Best GAA Jersey Ever|publisher=balls.ie| last=Mahoney|first=Donny|date= 4 December 2016|access-date=12 December 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sport.ucc.ie/about/history__trashed/the-real-story-behind-the-skull-and-crossbones/|title=The Real Story Behind The Skull And Crossbones|publisher=UCC Sport|access-date=12 December 2021|archive-date=23 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923005010/https://sport.ucc.ie/about/history__trashed/the-real-story-behind-the-skull-and-crossbones/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''Kilmallock GAA''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Kilmallock]], [[County Limerick]], Ireland. The club is primarily concerned with the game of [[hurling]], but has also fielded teams in other [[Gaelic games]].

==History==

Located in the town of [[Kilmallock]], about 20 miles outside [[Limerick (city)|Limerick]], Kilmallock GAA Club was founded in 1885.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://irelandxo.com/ireland-xo/history-and-genealogy/timeline/foundation-kilmallock-gaa-club|title=Foundation of Kilmallock GAA Club|publisher=IrelandXO|date=|access-date=3 June 2025}}</ref> Kilmallock's earliest successes where in [[Gaelic football]], with the club claiming [[Limerick Senior Football Championship|Limerick SFC]] titles in 1908, 1909 and 1916.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.milfordgaa.com/foundation-and-early-years|title=Foundation and Early Years|publisher=Milford GAA website|date=|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url = http://www.limerickcity.ie/media/olj%20vol%2050%20p162%20to%20163.pdf | title = Limerick GAA in 1916 | journal = The Old Limerick Journal | volume = 50 | date = 2016 }}</ref> Kilmallock made the hurling breakthrough in 1956 when they won the [[Limerick Junior Hurling Championship|Limerick JHC]] title and earned promotion to the senior grade.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-20210015.html|title=’Small town, good hurlers’|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=6 October 2012|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref>

Four years after that initial junior triumph, Kilmallock won the [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|Limerick SHC]] title after a defeat of [[Claughaun GAA|Claughaun]] in 1960.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-40728309.html|title='Some people might not like me saying this, but Patrickswell-Kilmallock is a real traditional final'|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=24 October 2021|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref> A second Limerick SHC title followed in 1967, before Kilmallock claimed three successive titles between 1973 and 1975.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/home/286270/kilmallock-s-hurling-heroes-reelin-the-year-1967-with-pride.html|title=Kilmallock's hurling heroes reel in the year 1967 with pride|publisher=Limerick Live|date=10 December 2017|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/gaelic-games/141636/Limerick-SHC-Final---Kilmallock.html|title=Limerick SHC Final - Kilmallock’s three-in-a-row success is fondly remembered|publisher=Limerick Live|date=5 October 2012|access-date=26 April 2025}}</ref> The club also won [[Munster Senior Club Hurling Championship|Munster Club SHC]] titles in 1992 and 1994, as well as losing to [[Sarsfields GAA (Galway)|Sarsfields]] in the [[1993 All-Ireland Senior Club Hurling Championship final|1993 All-Ireland club final]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://munster.gaa.ie/history/shclub_teams/|title=Senior Hurling (Club)|publisher=Munster GAA website|date=|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=|last=|archive-date=25 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225161148/http://munster.gaa.ie/history/shclub_teams/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/limerick-sport/128541/1992--When-Kilmallock-conquered-Limerick.html|title=1992: When Kilmallock conquered Limerick and Munster|publisher=Limerick Live|date=20 November 2014|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=|last=}}</ref>

The new century saw Kilmallock secure a number of underage titles in the minor and under-21 grades.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/community/117868/Parish-of-Kilmallock-behind-hurlers-as.html|title=Parish of Kilmallock behind hurlers as final looms|publisher=Limerick Live|date=16 March 2015|accessdate=6 October 2019|first=|last=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url = https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/sport/312390/kilmallock-impress-to-win-limerick-u-21-hurling-title-over-doon.html| website = Limerick Leader | publisher = Limerick Leader | title = Kilmallock impress to win Limerick U-21 hurling title over Doon | date = 9 May 2018 | accessdate = 23 August 2022 }}</ref> The club also won three Limerick SHC titles in a five-year period between 2010 and 2014, as well as a third Munster Club SHC title in 2014<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/delight-for-sparrow-as-kilmallock-defy-odds-292135.html|title=Delight for 'Sparrow' as Kilmallock defy odds|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=19 October 2014|access-date=4 August 2018|first=Jackie|last=Cahill}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/football/kilmallock-find-extra-gear-in-final-epic-299265.html|title=Kilmallock find extra gear in final epic|publisher=Irish Examiner|date=23 November 2014|access-date=4 August 2018}}</ref> Kilmallock also had a 1-18 to 1-06 defeat by [[Ballyhale Shamrocks GAA|Ballyhale Shamrocks]] in the [[2015 All-Ireland Senior Cl

'''Liam Mellows GAA''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club located in [[Renmore]], a suburb of [[Galway (city)|Galway City]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]].  The club is primarily concerned with the game of [[hurling]] and [[camogie]]. The club is named after IRB member [[Liam Mellows]].

On 12 November 2017, Liam Mellows reached their first [[Galway Senior Hurling Championship]] final since 1970 after defeating [[Cappataggle GAA|Cappataggle]] by 0-13 to 1-9 in Athenry.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hoganstand.com/Hurling/ArticleForm.aspx?ID=277984 |title=Galway SHC: Mellows reach first final in 47 years|date=12 November 2017|work=Hogan Stand|accessdate=15 November 2017}}</ref> 
On 3 December 2017 they beat [[Gort GAA|Gort]] to win the [[2017 Galway Senior Hurling Championship|championship]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irishexaminer.com/breakingnews/sport/liam-mellows-shock-gort-to-claim-galway-senior-hurling-title-816929.html |title=Liam Mellows shock Gort to claim Galway Senior Hurling title|date=3 December 2017|work=Irish Examiner|accessdate=4 December 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-games/hurling/liam-mellows-boss-explains-how-134-training-sessions-helped-bridge-47year-gap-to-galway-success-36375843.html |title=Liam Mellows boss explains how 134 training sessions helped bridge 47-year gap to Galway success|date=3 December 2017|work=Irish Independent|accessdate=4 December 2017}}</ref>

They were defeated by the All Ireland Champions [[Cuala CLG|Cuala]] in the semi-final in [[Thurles]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Club champs too strong for Mellows|url=http://www.advertiser.ie/galway/article/98631/club-champs-too-strong-for-mellows|work=[[Galway Advertiser]]}}</ref>

On 21 October 2023, Liam Mellows GAA club won their first Galway Junior A Camogie Championship. [[Niamh McPeake]] was named the "player of the game".<ref name="Website-1">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2023-10-21 |title=Junior A Final: Liam Mellows v Kiltormer |url=https://galwaycamogie.ie/2023-junior-a-final-liam-mellows-v-kiltormer/ |access-date=2026-10-27 |website=Galway Camogie |language=en-GB}}</ref>

}}'''Old Christians GAA''' club is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Limerick]], Ireland. It was formed in 1962 for the development of the games of [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]] in the southern part of Limerick city. Since then, the club has gone on to develop a number of league and championship winning teams at all level and has contributed a number of players to Limerick County teams. These include [[Bernie Hartigan]], who won an [[All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship]] with Limerick in 1973, and [[Ger Hegarty]], who won a Munster title and a [[National Hurling League]] medal in the mid-1990s.

==Location==
The club is centred on Our Lady Queen of Peace parish which is a working-class parish on the southside of [[Limerick City]]. Its players also come from Our Lady of Lourdes and Holy Family parishes. The main areas that provide players include Rathbane, Janesboro, Kennedy Park, Prospect, Ballinacurra Weston, Roxboro and Southill.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |title=OLD CHRISTIANS GAA CLUB |url=https://www.oldchristiansgaa.com |access-date=2025-05-06 |website=OLD CHRISTIANS GAA CLUB |language=en}}</ref>

==History==
Prior to the foundation of the club, sportsmen of the area played with [[South Liberties GAA]] or other city clubs such as the Commercials, Young Irelanders or [[Claughaun GAA]]. The club was originally set up in 1962 both to provide a GAA club for past pupils of Sexton Street CBS - hence the name 'Old Christians' whilst also helping to promote and foster hurling and Gaelic football on the southside of Limerick city in an area where rugby and in particular soccer are extremely popular.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}} Though they won the 1962 [[Limerick Senior Football Championship]] in their first year with victory over Claughaun and went on to win both Minor County Championships in hurling and football in 1966.<ref name="auto"/>

The clubs main concern was and has been hurling ever since, with their under-14 team winning the All-Ireland [[Féile na nGael]] title in 1972 beating [[Nenagh Éire Óg GAA]] in the final. They continued to hurl at a senior level up to the mid 1970s when the club went into decline as Sexton Street CBS began to decline in its prominence as a hurling nursery meaning less and less past pupils went on to play for 'Christians'.

The 1980s saw a revival,{{citation needed|date=July 2024}} and the club won several underage city and county titles. The minor hurlers reached the county final in 1984 under the Southill/Old Christians name. Old Christians won the 1992 County Intermediate Hurling Championship, but they struggled to compete at senior level and were often fought relegation.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}} They were eventually relegated to the intermediate grade in 1999, and they were back to playing junior A by 2007. At the underage level, they have won several county titles, including the County Under-14 A Football title in 2013.<ref name="auto"/> At adult level, they field a Junior A hurling team, but the club is without football team with sister club Ballinacurra Gaels catering for the area's football.

The club has struggled again in recent years but once again Christians appear to be rebuilding. In 2023 they won promotion to the Limerick Junior A Premier hurling championship, the fifth tier of Limerick club hurling. Christian's have also amalgamated with local junior clubs [[St Patrick's GAA (Limerick)|St Patrick's]] and [[Claughaun GAA|Claughaun]] at underage under the umbrella name of Southside Gaels.

==Grounds==
Old Christians have been playing at various locations around the Rathbane area since their foundation in 1962. The club's original home was Cannon Punch Park on the Hyde Road in Ballinacurra Weston, currently Hyde Rangers FC grounds. The current club grounds, Rathbane playing fields were formerly used by the CBS for athletics, PE, and hurling. Christians bought the  Rathbane site from Limerick City Council in the early 2000s and now have two full sized pitches along with a clubhouse containing a sports hall and gym and dressing rooms.

In 2022, the Rathbane playing pitches were renamed as Power Park in honour of the club's founding member John Power. Since then, Power Park become a venue for the [[Limerick Senior Football Championship]] on a number of occasions.

'''Newcastle West GAA''' club is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club located in [[Newcastle West]], [[County Limerick]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club was founded in 1887 and fields teams in [[Hurling]], [[Camogie]] and [[Gaelic football]].

==History==
Caisleain Nua Thiar Gaa Club was founded in 1897. Its early years were lean as Newcastle West did not emerge until 1908, when it reached the [[Limerick Senior Football Championship|Senior final]] with [[Kilmallock GAA|Kilmallock]], losing 2-08 to 0-3. Newcastle West footballers were still playing senior football through the 1900s up to 1928, where [[Glin, County Limerick|Glin]] beat them in the west final of that year by 0-12 to 0-01.

As a hurling club, they had no success prior to [[World War I]]. However from 1917 to 1933, Newcastle West were a force to be reckoned with, winning west titles and contesting 7 senior county finals during this period, winning in 1917 vs. Young Irelands (3-4 to 3-1) and in 1925 vs. Buff (3-2 to 1-2). The 1918 decider vs. Claughan was not played and they played second fiddle to Young Irelands in 1920 (5-4 to 1-1), Claughan in 1926 (1-4 to 5-3), and Young Irelands again both in 1930 (2-2 to 1-4) and 1932 (1-3 to 2-6). Their golden age in top flight Hurling ended in 1932. The late 1930s they found success for minor hurlers, winning a first county title in that grade, beating Claughan 7-5 to 0-1, and they reclaimed the County Junior Football title in 1938 beating Killmallock 0-4 to 0-3.

The 1940s began with a win in a West minor hurling title, while losing the county final to [[Ahane GAA|Ahane]] (6-1 to 3-1). This title, along with a West Junior Football title in 1945, were its only successes on the GAA Field until 1949, when another minor hurling team won a west title.

In the 1950s they met success in the west, both in minor hurling and football and junior football.{{Citation needed|date=June 2019}} The major change was the acquisition and development of the field in the Demesne.

In the 1960s they won the County junior final, beating Monaleen 2-2 to 2-0, and the club continued this success on the football field with a win in the West minor final in 1962, beating Abbeyfeale 3-5 to 2-7 and in 1965 winning the U21 beating [[Glin GAA|Glin]] 2-3 to 0-4. A fourth County junior football title was secured in 1966, beating St Patrick’s 1-12 to 1-5. Progress was also made in the game of hurling, winning west minor titles in 1960, 1961 and 1965.

Bord Na N'og emerged in the 1970s, for under-16s. They won a county U21 Football Championship in 1975, beating Na Piarsaigh 1-6 to 1-5. Newcastle won West Senior Football titles in 1971 and 1972, beating Glin and Askeaton, respectively. The footballers lost the county Senior Football title in 1972 to Askeaton.

In the 1980s, the club enjoyed success in hurling and football field with many dual stars. These players won a number of county titles including Minor Hurling in 1982, Minor football in 1980 and 1983, U21 hurling in 1985, U21 football in 1980, 1981, 1983, 1984 and 1987 and the Senior county football title in 1987. In the juvenile section, after the success of the 1980s hurling declined and the club went from senior to junior. Football remained strong and it won a second county title in 1992 along with multiple west championships. The hurling decline was later addressed by winning Juvenile County’s through the 1990s in all age groups.

The club celebrated a county junior hurling win in 2001. They experienced success at under-age level through the 2000s{{Citation needed|date=June 2019}}. A county senior football appearance in 2004 was followed by relegation in 2005. However a county Intermediate Football final win was celebrated in 2006. Through the late 2000s, success came in both minor hurling and football along with U-21 football. The senior footballers contested the Senior County Football Finals of 2011 and 2012, losing in 2011 to Monaleen and in 2012 to Drom-Broadford after a replay. In 2012, the club scored Junior B County Football League and Championship double and Premier Under-21 Football titles. The club also won two more u21 premier Football Championships, feeding the senior footballers with an extremely talented group of players for the coming years. In 2015 Newcastle won their first senior title in 23 years with a 2-10 to 0-9 win over [[Dromcollogher/Broadford GAA|Drom-Broadford]]. On 27 October 2019, the club's senior footballers won their fourth county senior championship title, defeating Oola. On 22 December 2019, the under-21 footballers won the U21 Premier Football Championship, completing the first back-to-back at this level since 1987/88. The club reached the premier intermediate grade in hurling for the first time ever, winning the 2020 County Intermediate Championship final against Na Piarsaigh.

'''Pallasgreen GAA''' club is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Pallasgreen]]/Templebraden parish in east [[County Limerick]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club was founded in 1887 and is a dual club fielding teams in both [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]].

==Location==
The club is situated in the parish of Pallasgreen/Templebraden and is a member of the East Board of [[Limerick GAA]]. The club is centred on the villages of [[Pallasgreen]], Old Pallas, Nicker and Barna. The parish is roughly 22 km southeast of [[Limerick City]] and just 8 km from the border with [[County Tipperary]]. Neighbouring clubs are Kilteely/Dromkeen, [[Caherline GAA|Caherline]], Caherconlish, [[Cappamore GAA|Cappamore]], [[Doon GAA|Doon]], Oola and Knockane. Knockane is the other GAA club situated in the southern half of the parish around the townlands of Knockane, Garrydoolis, Templebraden, Ballyneety and Sarsfield's Rock. Knockane fields Junior B hurling and football teams and has no underage structure. All juveniles therefore play with Pallasgreen and anyone living in the Knockane area can still play with Pallasgreen under the parish rule.

==History==
The club was founded in 1887 in an area where [[Gaelic games]] had been played since before the foundation of the GAA in 1884.{{fact|date=July 2024}} A Pallasgreen team beat Abbeyfeale in a tournament final at Corcanree. They competed in tournaments at various locations in [[County Limerick]] and many from the parish played with Knockane which had already been founded in 1884. The club was formed as 'New Pallas Milesians'. During those early years, Pallas, Knockane and Oola were all strong and players often interchanged between clubs.{{fact|date=July 2024}} In 1898, Pallas contested their only [[Limerick Senior Football Championship]] where they were defeated by the Commercials. However, in 1911 they beat [[South Liberties GAA|South Liberties]] in the County Intermediate Football Championship final. The club almost solely played football up to 1914 when a junior hurling team was formed. That team won the County Junior Hurling Championship the following year, beating Granagh in the final.{{fact|date=July 2024}}

==Achievements==

* '''[[Limerick Junior Hurling Championship]]''' (4) 1915, 1958, 1968, 1988
* '''Limerick Intermediate Football Championship''' (2) 2005, 2012

'''Young Irelands GAA''' was a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club based in [[Limerick City|Limerick]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club fielded both underage and adult male sports teams in [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]]. Founded in 1898, it was one of the most successful clubs in the city during the early 20th century, winning seven [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship]] titles between 1902 and 1932. After a period of decline starting in the 1980s, the club eventually disbanded in 1991.

==Formation==

On 16 November 1898, Young Irelands GAA was established as a boys underage [[hurling]] club in  Limerick. The first meeting was held at the headquarters of the Young Ireland Society. The club was named after the [[Young Ireland movement]]. The attendees at that meeting were Johnny Sweeny, Michael McInerney, James Fitzgerald, Jack Murphy, Pat Cowhey, Jim O’Connell,  Paddy O’Farrell, Frank O’Shaughnessy, and Jim Gleeson.

After the first few years interest developed into having a men's team.  The new team attracted players from the  Shamrocks club, along with adult members of the IRB and of the Young Ireland Society.

In 1902, Young Irelands defeated Monagea to win the first of their seven County Senior Hurling Championships. The six men who won both county titles were James Flanagan, Michael Hogan, Johnny Sweeny, Andy Kelly, M. Slattery and C. Kelly. In later years, Young Irelands won their second senior title in 1910 when they defeated [[Castleconnell]].

==Social Club==

In 1929, Young Irelands officially opened their club rooms. Young Irelands rented the rooms off the [[Gaelic League]], which had moved out.

Young Irelands GAA hosted lectures, concerts, and a weekly ceilidh in these rooms. The clubhouse facilities included a library and billiard tables. Following their 1928 victory against [[Rathkeale]], the club held a banquet at Cruises Hotel; they were the first club to host such an event to honor a County Championship success.

==Golden Era==

During the 1920s, Young Irelands GAA frequently played [[Claughaun GAA|Claughaun]], which was headquartered in the same building. Young Irelands trained and played matches at the [[Markets Field]] during this era. Near the end of the season, Young Irelands and [[Garryowen Rugby Club|Garryowen]] often trained at opposite ends of the field simultaneously.

Young Irelands defeated Newcastlewest in 1920, [[Bruff]] in 1922 and Rathkeale in 1928 to capture their fifth County Senior hurling title. In 1927, Young Ireland organized a seven-a-side hurling confined to club members.  The team held committee meetings in the Gaelic League Hall every Wednesday.

During 1902 Young Ireland GAA rented a field in Roxboro Road.  However, in 1932, due to housing development nearby, the club moved back to  Markets Field. Due to rent increase, the club also moved to new quarters at Number 8 The Crescent in 1932 for an annual rent of £100.

In 1930. Young Irelands won the County senior hurling championship, defeating Newcastlewest. They defeated Newcastlewest again in 1932 to capture their last county title.

During the 1930s Young Irelands fielded Senior hurling teams in both Cork and Limerick on the same Sunday . In Cork they played St Finbarrs and at Limericks Gaelic Grounds they lined out another 15 against [[Cappamore]]. On another occasion, they travelled by train to [[Killarney]], toured the Lakes, played a senior hurling match against Corks Glen Rovers and a Senior Football match against the local Dr. Crokes.

In 1921, Killaloe-born Bob Mc Conkey lifted the Liam McCarthy<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gaa.ie |date=2023-07-18 |title=A century of the Liam MacCarthy Cup |url=https://www.gaa.ie/hurling/news/a-century-of-the-liam-maccarthy-cup |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=www.gaa.ie |language=en}}</ref> while in 1923 [[Paddy McInerney]], who was born in O’Callaghan's Mills but who moved to Limerick at a young age, captained the side.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2009-05-29 |title=Senior Hurling - Munster GAA |url=https://munster.gaa.ie/history/hurling/senior-hurling/ |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=Munster GAA - Aras Mumhan |language=en}}</ref> In 1932, [[Caherconlish]]-born Mickey Fitzgibbon captained the Limerick side. Mick Kennedy originally from The Ragg in Tipperary captained the side that won Limericks First National hurling league title in 1933–34. Mick Murphy, Willie Gleeson, Paddy McInerney, Denny Lanigan, Bob McConkey, Mick Kennedy all won All Ireland Senior hurling medals with Limerick.<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Connell |first=Jerome |date=2018-05-25 |title=Relatives sought for re-enactment of Limerick's 1918 All Ireland hurling final win |url=https://www.limerickleader.ie/news/sport/314807/relatives-sought-for-re-enactment-of-limerick-s-1918-all-ireland-hurling-final-win.html |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=www.limerickleader.ie |language=en}}</ref>

'''Shinrone GAA Club''' is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] club in [[Shinrone]], [[County Offaly]], [[Ireland]]. The club is almost exclusively concerned with the game of [[hurling]].

==History==

Located in the village of [[Shinrone]], on the [[County Offaly|Offaly]]-[[County Tipperary|Tipperary]] border, Shinrone GAA Club was one of the first seventy clubs affiliated to [[GAA Central Council|Central Council]] after the foundation of the [[Gaelic Athletic Association|GAA]] in 1884. Hurling and [[Gaelic football]] had been played in the area prior to this.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.shinronegaa.ie/club-history|title=Club History|publisher=Shinrone GAA website|date=|access-date=1 September 2024|first=|last=}}</ref>

The club has spent most of its existence operating in the junior grade and are the all-time record-holders, having won nine [[Offaly Junior A Hurling Championship|Offaly JHC]] titles over a 100-year period. Shinrone have also won four [[Offaly Intermediate Hurling Championship|Offaly IHC]] titles at various intervals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hoganstand.com/offaly/ClubTitles|title=Club Titles - Offaly|publisher=Hogan Stand|date=|access-date=1 September 2024|first=|last=}}</ref>

Shinrone qualified for their very first [[Offaly Senior Hurling Championship#List of finals|Offaly SHC final]] in [[1960 Offaly Senior Hurling Championship#Final|1960]], however, they lost to [[Drumcullen GAA|Drumcullen]] by a point.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.offalyexpress.ie/news/home/922828/painful-memories-of-the-one-that-got-away-in-1960-and-how-emigration-ended-shinrone-s-golden-generation.html|title=Painful memories of the one that got away in 1960 and how emigration ended Shinrone's golden generation|publisher=Offaly Live|date=30 September 2022|access-date=28 August 2025|first=|last=}}</ref> The club claimed their inaugural [[Offaly Senior Hurling Championship|Offaly SHC]] after a 0–26 to 2–13 win over [[Kilcormac–Killoughey GAA|Kilcormac–Killoughey]] in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/gaelic-games/hurling/shinrone-make-history-with-first-offaly-shc-title-after-emphatic-win-over-kilmormackilloughey-42033980.html|title=Shinrone make history with first Offaly SHC title after emphatic win over Kilmormac/Killoughey|publisher=Irish Independent|date=2 October 2022|access-date=2 October 2022|first=|last=}}</ref>

==History==

The original [[Mungret GAA|Mungret]] club was one of the first clubs formed in [[County Limerick|Limerick]] after the establishment of the [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] in 1884. The club was very much to the fore in the early days of the GAA but, like many other clubs of the time, the Parnell split took its toll on club membership with the result that the club disbanded. The club was eventually reformed under the Mungret/St. Paul's banner in 1929, by the then headmaster of Mungret national school, Mr. P. J. ''' St Patrick's GAA''' ([[Irish language|Irish]]: ''CLG Naomh Pádraig'') is a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] located in the Rhebogue area of [[Limerick City]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The club fields teams in both [[hurling]] and [[Gaelic football]].

==History==

Located in the Rhebogue area on the banks of the [[River Shannon]], St Patrick's GAA Club is one of the oldest clubs in Limerick, having been founded in 1886.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.limerick.ie/discover/eat-see-do/sports-recreation/sports-clubs-classes/gaa/saint-patricks-gaa-club |title=Saint Patrick's GAA Club|publisher=Limerick website|access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref> It remains the oldest-surviving city club. The club had several successes in Gaelic football in its early years, winning back-to-back [[Limerick Senior Football Championship|Limerick SFC]] titles at the expense of [[Commercials GAA (Limerick)|Commercials]] in 1890 and 1891. Half a century passed before the club enjoyed what could arguably be described as its most successful period.{{or-inline|date=July 2024}} Further Limerick SFC titles were won in 1943, 1944 and 1954, while St Patrick's also claimed consecutive [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|Limerick SHC]] titles in 1949 and 1950.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hoganstand.com/Limerick/ClubTitles|title=Club titles - Limerick|publisher=Hogan Stand|access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref> The club's most recent success was a [[Limerick Junior Hurling Championship|Limerick JAHC]] title in 2017. The club recently completed the building of a new club house in May 2024.

'''Western Gaels GAA''' was a [[Gaelic Athletic Association]] division located in west [[County Limerick]], [[Republic of Ireland|Ireland]]. The division fielded teams in both [[Gaelic football]] and [[hurling]].

==History==

Divisional Boards in Limerick were created at the start of the 20th century, with the West Board being formed in 1902. The notion of divisional teams taking part in the [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|SHC]] and [[Limerick Senior Football Championship|SFC]] is believed to have first been suggested in the late 1940s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vsopublicationsltd.ie/down-memory-lane-four-county-titles-for-western-gaels-in-a-glorious-ten-year-spell/|title=Down Memory Lane – Four county titles for Western Gaels in a glorious ten year spell|publisher=Vale Star|date=4 June 2020|access-date=31 October 2024}}</ref> These divisional teams would be composed of players from the various juvenile and intermediate clubs within the division. The divisional system had been operated by [[Cork GAA]] in their competitions since the 1930s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.irishexaminer.com/sport/gaa/arid-41495513.html|title=Watch: Denis Ring on Cork divisional debate — 'It was never raised as a question until Imokilly started to win'|date=14 October 2024|publisher=Irish Examiner|access-date=31 October 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.echolive.ie/corksport/arid-41577367.html|title=Reform or removal: The age old debate around divisions in Cork GAA|date=21 February 2025|publisher=Echo Live|access-date=22 April 2025}}</ref>

Western Gaels, as the division became known as, had a successful period between 1953 and 1962. During that time the team contested six senior finals in Gaelic football and hurling. Western Gaels won SFC titles in 1953 and 1954, before claiming consecutive SHC titles in 1961 and 1962.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://limerickgaa.ie/granagh-ballingarry-gaa-club-notes-36/|title=Granagh-Ballingarry GAA Club notes|publisher=Limerick GAA website|date=22 April 2021|access-date=31 October 2024}}</ref> They also narrowly missed out on completing [[The Double (Gaelic games)|the double]] in 1961.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hoganstand.com/Limerick/ClubTitles|title=Club titles - Limerick|publisher=Hogan Stand|access-date=15 October 2018}}</ref>

==Honours==

* [[Limerick Senior Hurling Championship]] (2): [[1961 Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|1961]], [[1962 Limerick Senior Hurling Championship|1962]]
* [[Limerick Senior Football Championship]] (2): 1953, 1960
